episode_title: The Oranges and the Colonies: What the King's Own Study Found
description: A study King Willem-Alexander asked for and paid for finds that the House of Orange actively backed colonialism for centuries and earned the equivalent of about 576 million euros from it. Prime Minister Rob Jetten has ruled out new reparations. Also today: inflation is up again and the G7 is releasing emergency diesel, a court backs stricter family reunification rules, banks cut how much older buyers can borrow, vapes get a planned tax, and Dutch television turns 75.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: For centuries, every Dutch stadtholder, king and queen, at least up to Queen Wilhelmina, believed colonialism was legitimate. They backed it, and they profited from it.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That isn't coming from activists or critics, either. It comes from a study the King asked for and paid for himself.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Today, the royal family's colonial past, what the King said about it, and why the government says there won't be new reparations. It's Saturday, the 3rd of October. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I'm Sam. And this is Dutch Daily Briefing.

segments.title: The House of Orange and colonialism

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: On Friday, at Leiden University's Academy Building, King Willem-Alexander was handed a huge piece of research. It runs to five volumes and about two thousand pages, and it covers his own family's role in Dutch colonial history.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Quick bit of background for newcomers. The House of Orange-Nassau is the Dutch royal family, and people here usually just call them the Oranges. Before there was a king, the country was a republic, and the Oranges were stadtholders, a kind of hereditary leader.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: About sixty researchers worked on it, led by historian Gert Oostindie. His conclusion was blunt. He says the family gave colonialism what he called active and unscrupulous support for centuries. That included slavery for as long as it existed, and the violent crushing of uprisings.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And then there's the money. The researchers put the family's earnings at nearly 576 million euros in today's money.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Where did it come from?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Nearly all of it came from the East. That means the VOC, the Dutch East India Company, which was a trading company with its own armies, and later the Dutch East Indies, which is now Indonesia. Around half a billion came in the nineteenth century alone. You may have seen headlines saying the money came from slavery. The researchers put it differently. It came from colonialism. The family made almost nothing from the transatlantic slave trade.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: But not because they objected.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: No. It was because the West India Company, which ran that trade, lost them money.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Does the family still have that wealth?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: According to the researchers, very little of it. Stadtholder William the Fifth fled the country penniless in 1795, and later fortunes were lost on investments in Tsarist Russia and the Habsburg empire.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The study also asks how much power the royals actually had over colonial policy.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Mostly not much. The Netherlands is a constitutional monarchy, so elected governments make policy. The big exception was King William the First, in the early 1800s. He largely ran colonial policy himself, and in 1828 he looked for ways around the laws against the slave trade.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The study calls Queen Wilhelmina the most imperialist monarch of them all. She backed the Aceh War, and she backed the military campaign against Indonesian independence. In 1947 she wrote that she had no objection to what were then called police actions. The first criticism of colonialism from the palace didn't come until Queen Juliana, in 1948.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So how did the King react?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: He called the findings heartbreaking and confronting, and said they affect him. He also said, quote, I cannot change the past, but I can make a positive contribution to the present and the future. He called the report not a conclusion but a call to action.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Did he say anything about money, or some kind of repair?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: No. And at his weekly press conference, Prime Minister Rob Jetten ruled out new reparations. He pointed to the 200 million euros the government set aside in 2023 for awareness, remembrance and education, and to plans to return colonial-era art.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That money came out of the government's apology for slavery in 2022. Then, on Keti Koti in 2023, the day the abolition of slavery is commemorated, the King apologised himself. He's also stopped using the Golden Coach because one of its panels shows colonial scenes. The researchers say no other European monarch has gone that far.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Reactions to the report were mixed. NiNsee, the national institute for the history and legacy of Dutch slavery, welcomed it and called for talks on repair. A foundation representing Indigenous people from Suriname and the Caribbean said they'd been overlooked once again. And activist Mitchell Esajas, co-founder of The Black Archives, gave back the royal honour he received in 2023. He said words about reconciliation aren't enough while economic and racial inequality persists.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: If you want to read it yourself, the research is published by Boom. There's also an English-language book comparing European monarchs and colonialism, and a version of the main book written for the general public.

segments.title: Inflation rises and the G7 opens its emergency oil reserves

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Now to your wallet. Dutch inflation went up again in September, to 3.4 percent, according to a first estimate from CBS, the national statistics bureau.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's a small rise from August. The main driver is energy. Motor fuel and heating cost almost fourteen percent more than a year ago, and electricity is now more expensive than last year too.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: There is some better news. Groceries got a bit cheaper for the second month in a row.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Enjoy that while it lasts. CBS chief economist Peter Hein van Mulligen says high energy prices usually show up in shop prices about six months later. He doesn't expect a spike like 2022, though.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: For newer listeners, 2022 was when energy prices after Russia's invasion of Ukraine pushed Dutch inflation into double digits. Across the eurozone, inflation is now 3.8 percent, its highest since September 2023. Before the war in Iran began, it was just under two percent.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And at the pump, the advisory prices for diesel and petrol are above 2.70 a litre. To be fair, the average price people actually pay is lower than that.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Meanwhile the G7 countries have agreed to release up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from emergency reserves over the next four months. A big share of the diesel is meant to come out in the first twenty days.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Why now?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It followed pressure from President Trump. He'd threatened to ban US diesel exports to bring prices down at home ahead of the midterm elections. That would really hurt here, because Europe now gets a lot of its diesel from the US.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So Europe agreed to open its own reserves before that could happen. European diesel futures dropped about eight percent after the announcement.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The Netherlands isn't in the G7, but it's already drawing on its reserves under an earlier international deal from March. On Thursday the cabinet released another batch, mostly diesel and petrol, which brings it close to what it pledged. It hasn't said whether it'll add more under the new G7 deal.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And on fuel tax, don't expect a new cut. On Budget Day, the cabinet chose to phase out the existing excise discount more slowly in 2027. That stops a planned price rise, but it doesn't lower anything.

segments.title: Court backs stricter family reunification rules

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Next, a court ruling that matters to thousands of families. The district court in The Hague has ruled that stricter rules on bringing relatives to the Netherlands also apply to applications filed before those rules took effect.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Let's set this up. Since the 12th of June, when the EU Asylum and Migration Pact took effect, the Netherlands has had what's called a two-status system. Recognised refugees are on one track. People with subsidiary protection, meaning they aren't recognised as refugees but can't safely go home, are on a stricter one.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And for that second group, family reunification is now much harder. They have to wait two years before they can apply, and they need housing that's suitable for the whole family.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The law has no transitional arrangement. So people who had already applied under the old rules suddenly found the new ones applied to them.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's what happened to the two Syrians who brought this case. The IND, the immigration service, turned down their requests under the new conditions. The court acknowledged the effects can be serious, especially for people who applied under the old rules. But it found that neither the rules nor applying them to older cases breaks higher law or general legal principles.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: How many people are we talking about?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: When the rules took effect, more than nineteen thousand people were waiting for a decision on family reunification. It's not yet clear how many of them have subsidiary protection.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And this is the first ruling on the new rules, so it's not the end of it.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: No. The lawyer will appeal, and the refugee charity VluchtelingenWerk says the Council of State, the top court for cases against the government, will have the final word. No date has been set for that ruling yet.

segments.title: Banks cut mortgages for older buyers

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: If you're in your fifties and thinking about buying or refinancing, this one's for you. Rabobank and ABN Amro are cutting how much older customers can borrow.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Here's how it works. Your maximum mortgage depends on your income. Pension income is usually lower than a salary. So the earlier a bank starts counting your pension instead of your salary, the less you can borrow.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: From March, Rabobank and its subsidiary Obvion will start counting expected pension income fifteen years before retirement instead of ten. With the retirement age at 67, that affects applicants from age 52. Rabobank will also factor in life expectancy. Borrowers aged 85 and over will be able to borrow at most seventy percent of their home's value.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And ABN Amro?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: ABN Amro brings in similar changes on the 9th of December, including its Florius label. It's keeping the ten-year threshold, but it'll check whether your income after retirement is enough to cover the loan. At 85, it caps borrowing at half the home's value. If you're with Rabobank and you don't change your existing loan, these rules don't apply to you.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: This comes from new guidance by DNB, the Dutch central bank. ING hasn't announced anything yet, but others in the sector expect more lenders to follow.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's not yet clear exactly how much less a typical buyer in their mid-fifties will be able to borrow. But the data firm IEX says self-employed people with little pension saved will be hit hardest. Someone relying only on the state pension might qualify for a mortgage of about a hundred thousand euros.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: In this housing market, that doesn't buy you much.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Vapes are going to get more expensive. The government plans to add an excise tax on vapes and refills from January 2029, on top of the VAT people already pay.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The rate hasn't been set. The aim is to make vapes about as expensive as tobacco. The plan comes from Eelco Eerenberg of D66, the State Secretary for Finance, which is basically a junior minister in charge of taxes.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: He said it's shocking how many young people are vaping, and the numbers back him up. More than one in five secondary school pupils aged twelve to sixteen have tried it, and about one in eight vaped in the past month.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: He also had a good line: the health of our children cannot wait for Brussels. But he admits vapes are easy to buy online or across the border. That's why he'd still prefer a tax across the whole EU.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And if an EU tax arrives first, the Dutch one gets dropped. That doesn't look likely soon, though. EU tax rules need all twenty-seven countries to agree, and in June finance ministers took the plan off their agenda because they couldn't.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The Dutch bill should go to the Tweede Kamer, the House of Representatives, in early 2027. That's on top of the flavour ban that's been in place since 2024, which, honestly, a lot of shops ignore in practice.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Some local news from Amsterdam. The city has dropped its plan to make Utrechtsestraat one-way, Het Parool reports.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's the busy shopping and restaurant street running from Rembrandtplein across the canals to Frederiksplein. Trams, bikes, delivery vans and pedestrians all squeeze through it.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The city said the street was unsafe and carried more than four thousand vehicles a day. The plan was to keep southbound traffic on the street and send northbound traffic through side streets.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the neighbours didn't like that.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: They didn't. Residents' groups worried the traffic would just move onto their streets. They disputed the city's figures and did their own counts. In a neighbourhood survey, most respondents said the street felt safe and opposed the plan. The small-business group MKB Metropool Amsterdam was against it as well.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So what happens instead?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Smaller measures: an extra zebra crossing, changes at the Frederiksplein junction, checks on loading and on speeding, and speed bumps. It's still only a proposal. The Centrum district committee discusses it on Monday before a final decision.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Okay, time for some lighter stuff. Last night was the Dutch film world's big night out.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The Golden Calves! For newcomers, think of the Oscars and the Emmys rolled into one, handed out in Utrecht at the end of the Netherlands Film Festival. And yes, the trophy really is a little golden calf.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The big winner was Truly Naked, the first feature from director Muriel d'Ansembourg. It won six of its seven nominations, including best film and best director.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And it's in English, which makes it handy for our listeners. It's set in a British seaside town and follows Alec, a shy teenage boy growing up in his dad's low-budget porn business. It's about how pornography shapes teenage lives.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Not exactly a family film night, then.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: No, maybe not with the in-laws. But it's streaming now on Pathé Thuis and Picl.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Television also had a good night. Basta, the Videoland series about football legend Marco van Basten, won three awards, including best lead actor for Chris Peters.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Van Basten scored that famous volley in the 1988 European Championship final, which is still the Dutch team's only major title. If your Dutch colleagues ever go misty-eyed about a football goal, that's probably the one.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Meanwhile the favourite, Joe Speedboot, had nine nominations and won just one: best actor for Daan Buringa. And Halina Reijn, who directed Babygirl with Nicole Kidman, got a career award. She called herself a farmer's girl in Hollywood.

segments.title: Hans Anders pulls Meta's camera glasses

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Next, the Dutch optician chain Hans Anders has taken Meta's camera glasses off its shelves and its website, for now.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: These are the Ray-Ban glasses that look completely normal. But they can take photos and video hands-free, make calls and play music. A tiny light flickers while they're recording.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Which you'd only notice if you were looking very closely at someone's face.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Right, and that's the whole debate. Here they've been nicknamed the gluurbril, which means the peeping glasses. That tells you how people feel about them.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: This week Offlimits, a support group for victims of online abuse, and the campaign group The Firewall gave Meta two weeks to stop selling the glasses, or they'll go to court. NOS reports the Consumentenbond, the consumers' association, is involved too. On the same day, the Tweede Kamer passed a motion asking the cabinet to restrict wearing them, with exceptions for medical use.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The cabinet would rather wait for an EU assessment, which is expected this autumn. And Hans Anders says it only sold limited numbers. So if you really want a pair, Pearle, Specsavers and MediaMarkt are still selling them.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And finally, a birthday. Dutch television is 75 years old this week.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The first broadcast was ninety minutes, live, from a studio in Bussum. It was introduced by announcer Jeanne Roos and featured a live performance of a play called The Magic Mirror.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Hardly anyone owned a set. There were about five hundred in the whole country, each costing about a third of an average year's income. So people crowded around radio shop windows and in cafés. The royal family watched from Soestdijk Palace.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the government didn't really want TV at all. Prime Minister Willem Drees wanted money spent on housing, not luxuries. He worried television would distract workers and corrupt young people.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Then Father Kors, who headed the broadcasters, went on air during that very first broadcast and warned about television's harmful influence.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's a great first episode. Hello, welcome to television, and it's bad for you.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So why did it happen at all?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Philips, the electronics giant from Eindhoven, threatened to start television on its own. That got the government moving, and even then TV was approved only as a two-year experiment. It also explains something that confuses a lot of newcomers. Dutch public TV is split among lots of broadcasting associations, because Dutch society was once divided into Catholic, Protestant, socialist and liberal pillars, and each one got its own broadcaster.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Media historian Huub Wijfjes says TV peaked from the sixties to the eighties, when shows pulled in seven or eight million viewers. And he says it's still the dominant medium.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The two-year experiment is doing fine, then.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: But if you'd rather get away from screens tonight, here are some ideas.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: My pick is tonight at the Ziggo Dome in Zuidoost. The Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, conducted by Iván Fischer, is playing classical highlights in an arena. It starts at eight and finishes with Beethoven's Ninth.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And the whole audience gets to sing Ode to Joy.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Exactly. There's an optional sing-along rehearsal from seven, and ticket holders get practice material in advance. So no excuses.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: If you prefer cinema, Camera Japan is on at LAB111 in Oud-West. It's the biggest Japanese film festival in the Benelux, with arthouse, anime and classics, plus music, dance and food. It runs from half past twelve until ten tonight and finishes tomorrow. Times may change, so check their website.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And if you're up early, there's an antiques, curiosities and vintage market at the Oosterkerk in the eastern city centre, from nine until five. It's free to browse, and it's on today only.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's it for today's Dutch Daily Briefing. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I'm Sam. Have a great Saturday, and if you go tonight, practise your German vowels for that Ode to Joy.
